claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by formation of a stable nanocrystalline grain structure.
A nanocrystalline grain structure increases resistance to plastic deformation.
A nanocrystalline grain structure reduces crack propagation.
Increased grain-boundary area promotes grain-boundary sliding and rotation.
Grain-boundary sliding and rotation enhance plastic-deformation resistance and reduce crack propagation, thereby improving wear resistance.
The initial as-deposited or processed coatings have grain sizes of approximately 10–50 nm.
Heat treatment at 500 °C for 1 hour induces grain growth.
Heat treatment at 500 °C for 1 hour relaxes residual stresses.
The intervention also varies coating composition and deposition method.
Wear is tested under dry sliding at a normal load of 10 N and a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s.
The as-deposited baseline wear rate is 1 × 10^-4 mm^3/Nm.
The intervention will reduce wear rate by 25%, from 1 × 10^-4 to 7.5 × 10^-5 mm^3/Nm, relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The hypothesis applies to coatings with grain sizes between 20 and 50 nm.
The hypothesis applies at normal loads between 10 and 15 N.
The hypothesis applies at sliding speeds between 0.05 and 0.5 m/s.
Coating thickness, surface roughness, and environmental conditions may also influence wear performance.
Failure of the heat-treated coating to reduce wear rate by at least 20% relative to the as-deposited coating falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes improved wear resistance to retention of a stable nanocrystalline structure, but the intervention explicitly induces grain growth while predicting improved wear. No post-treatment grain size or rationale is given to show that the coating remains in the beneficial nanocrystalline range, and residual-stress relaxation is not integrated into the stated mechanism.

The nominal test simultaneously changes heat treatment, composition, and deposition method. This prevents a clean attribution of a wear-rate change to grain size or grain-boundary mechanisms alone and is inconsistent with a single controlled change.
